title: Anthropic ships Claude Code 'mods' — TypeScript hooks that can rewrite the agent from the inside
subtitle: Mods, released with Claude Code 2.1.287, let developers run small TypeScript functions before, after, or in place of prompt submissions, tool calls, permission requests, and UI renders — Anthropic rebuilt three of its own features as mods at launch.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic shipped Claude Code mods on October 1, tying the release to version 2.1.287 of its command-line tool. A mod is a small TypeScript function that hooks into Claude Code's internal event loop — it can run before, after, or in place of a prompt submission, a tool call, a permission request, or a UI render. Concretely, a mod can rewrite a prompt before the model sees it, block or retry a tool call, approve or deny a permission request, strip secrets out of tool output, or inject custom UI elements and new slash commands. Mods install through the existing /plugin command and work in both the CLI and the desktop app. Anthropic shipped three of its own built-in features — the diff pane, the agents.md loader, and telemetry — as mods at launch, to prove the extension surface was wide enough to replace core functionality.

The architectural choice is unusual for a frontier lab. Most agent frameworks hide the loop behind an API; Anthropic has exposed the loop itself as a programmable surface. That matters because the hard problems in agent engineering — redacting secrets, enforcing per-team permission policies, routing retries, logging to a corporate SIEM — happen between the model and the tool, not inside either one. Mods let a team solve those problems once and share the solution as a plugin, instead of forking Claude Code or wrapping it in a bespoke orchestration layer.

The security tradeoff is explicit and sharp. Mods run with the same machine privileges as Claude Code itself and are explicitly unsandboxed. Anthropic's own release notes treat an installed mod as equivalent to a locally installed program, with all the trust that implies. That is the correct call for a developer tool and a dangerous one for a widely distributed marketplace. Expect the first wave of mods to be internal tools inside enterprise security perimeters, and expect the first mod-based incident — a malicious mod silently exfiltrating a repo via a 'helper' panel — to arrive within months, not years.

A note for learners in developer tooling or AI engineering: this is the clearest invitation yet to build and share agent infrastructure as a product. If you have ever wished your coding agent redacted a specific API key format, enforced your team's commit convention, or added a one-click 'open PR' button in a particular way, mods are the shortest path from annoyance to shipped feature. The skill to practice is reading your agent's event stream — knowing exactly where in the loop your logic belongs is the whole craft. Treat the Anthropic blog's reference mods as the training set; the diff-pane rewrite in particular shows how a non-trivial feature decomposes into hooks.
